title: Area of Quadrilaterals

findings.finding: The half-diagonal questions require diagonal bisection properties that the preceding teaching does not explicitly supply.
findings.breakdown: Students must identify which diagonal is bisected before doubling the labelled half. They could instead substitute the half-length directly or assume both diagonals of every kite are bisected.
findings.checked: p3-diagonals explains endpoints; p4-kites and p4-rhombuses explain side properties. The p5 rearrangements illustrate particular halves but do not state how to identify the bisected diagonal generally. The p6 examples and guided practice and p7 identification tasks use complete diagonals. The targeted p9 diagrams supply side equality marks, not marks directly identifying equal half-diagonals.
findings.assumptions: The supplied teaching is complete. Recognising the required bisection property is a new variant of the diagonal work taught here; calculator availability does not affect it.

repair.proposal: Before p9-q3, add: “In a kite, the diagonal joining the vertices where the equal side pairs meet bisects the other diagonal. The first diagonal is not necessarily bisected. In a rhombus, both diagonals bisect each other. For example, if one half of a bisected diagonal is 7 cm, its complete length is 2×7=14 cm. Use the complete length in the area formula.”

findings.doneWhen: Before p9-q3-a, students have an explicit rule identifying the bisected diagonal and a modelled conversion from a half-diagonal to its complete length.

findings.finding: Extend the flying-kite question by changing the lower rod while keeping the other three rods fixed.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects complete diagonal length with area and distinguishes the lower rod from the whole vertical diagonal.
findings.checked: The horizontal diagonal remains 60 cm. A 90 cm lower rod gives a vertical diagonal of 120 cm and area 3600 cm². Twice the original 2700 cm² requires a vertical diagonal of 180 cm, hence a lower rod of 150 cm. Both configurations remain valid kites.
findings.assumptions: Use the original diagram and retain its perpendicular rods and three equal 30 cm rods.

repair.proposal: Append to p9-q4: (a) “The lower rod is lengthened from 60 cm to 90 cm. The other three rods remain 30 cm each. What area of plastic is now needed?” Answer: 3600 cm². (b) “Keeping those three rods at 30 cm each, how long must the lower rod be for the kite to have twice its original area?” Answer: 150 cm.

findings.doneWhen: The two optional follow-up parts use the original kite context and have the stated answers.

findings.finding: Vary the individual parallel-side lengths while holding their sum and the perpendicular height fixed.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes that trapezium area depends on the sum of the parallel sides rather than their difference.
findings.checked: The supplied teaching and practice contain no comparable consecutive run. Each proposed trapezium is valid. Parts d–f have area 4×12÷2=24 cm²; the unpatterned part has area 6×13÷2=39 cm².
findings.assumptions: Present the added parts as dimensioned trapeziums under the existing instruction.

repair.proposal: After p13-q1-c, add the single instruction “Predict each area before calculating.” Add parts with these parallel sides and perpendicular heights: d: 1 cm, 11 cm; height 4 cm. e: 3 cm, 9 cm; height 4 cm. f: 5 cm, 7 cm; height 4 cm. Answers: 24 cm² each. Follow with g: parallel sides 4 cm and 9 cm; height 6 cm. Answer: 39 cm².

findings.doneWhen: Three consecutive parts hold the parallel-side sum and height fixed, followed by the unpatterned part, with only the prediction line added.

findings.finding: The worked example substitutes a rectangle height of 8 cm without explaining its derivation from 13−5.
findings.breakdown: The diagram also labels the top width as 8 cm. Students can copy that visible value into the rectangle calculation without recognising that the rectangle height must be calculated from the total height.
findings.checked: Neither p18-example-original nor p18-example-decomposition prints the derived rectangle height. The displayed calculation starts directly with A₂=8×11. Earlier trapezium examples use supplied heights and do not supply this missing connection.
findings.assumptions: Diagram specifications describe geometric relationships but do not make unprinted calculations student-visible. Calculator availability does not affect the missing decision.

repair.proposal: Before A₂=8×11, insert: “Rectangle height = total height − trapezium height = 13−5 = 8 cm.”

findings.doneWhen: The worked example explicitly derives the rectangle height and distinguishes it from the equally valued top width.

findings.finding: Follow the composite-area question by redistributing the two triangle heights while retaining their sum.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up makes explicit why individual triangle heights are unnecessary when their bases are equal and their combined height is known.
findings.checked: Both proposed pairs of positive heights sum to 16 m and retain the original 24 m total span. The square contributes 64 m² and the triangles together contribute ½×8×16=64 m², giving 128 m² in both cases. Only the component-area methods already used in the topic are required.
findings.assumptions: Retain the central square and the two attached isosceles triangles from the original diagram.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p22-q8-b, add optional parts: (i) “The central square still has side 8 m. The left triangle has perpendicular height 5 m and the right triangle has perpendicular height 11 m. Find the total area.” Answer: 128 m². (ii) “Change the perpendicular heights to 7 m and 9 m. Find the total area.” Answer: 128 m². (iii) “Explain why the totals are equal.” Expected answer: the square is unchanged, and both triangles have base 8 m while their perpendicular heights still total 16 m, so their combined area remains 64 m².

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts separately ask for the two areas and one explanation of their equality.

findings.finding: Extend the square-diagonal comparison to expose how doubling or halving a diagonal changes area.
findings.breakdown: The numerical follow-up connects the diagonal-area calculation with a central area relationship.
findings.checked: A square is a rhombus with equal diagonals, so its area is d²/2. Diagonals of 40 cm and 10 cm give areas of 800 cm² and 50 cm². The first is four times the original 200 cm². The method is already available in p24-q4-b and the earlier rhombus teaching.
findings.assumptions: Students may use either method compared in the original question; no general proof or additional method is required.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p24-q4-b, add optional parts: c. “A second square has a diagonal of 40 cm. Find its area.” Answer: 800 cm². d. “How many times the area of the original square is this?” Answer: 4 times. e. “A third square has a diagonal of 10 cm. Find its area.” Answer: 50 cm².

findings.doneWhen: The three optional numerical parts follow the original comparison and have the stated answers.

protectedGroups.observation: Different valid partitions give the same total area and can be compared for convenience.
protectedGroups.invariant: The whole figure, its dimensions and its area.

protectedGroups.observation: The meaning of the measurements, rather than the shape name or numerical values, determines the usable formula.
protectedGroups.varies: The 5 cm and 4 cm measurements change from base and perpendicular height to complete diagonals.
protectedGroups.invariant: Both figures are rhombuses and use the same numerical values and formula choices.

protectedGroups.observation: The explicit comparison revisits the preceding formula distinction and connects it to areas of 20 cm² and 10 cm²; this instructional purpose justifies reuse of the earlier pair.
protectedGroups.varies: The roles of the 5 cm and 4 cm measurements.
protectedGroups.invariant: Rhombus classification and the numerical measurements.

protectedGroups.observation: The perpendicular height stays horizontal when the longer vertical parallel side switches sides.
protectedGroups.varies: Which vertical parallel side is longer and the direction of the sloping top.
protectedGroups.invariant: Vertical parallel sides and horizontal perpendicular separation.

protectedGroups.observation: Decomposition and the trapezium formula give the same area.
protectedGroups.invariant: The corresponding dimensions and total area.

protectedGroups.observation: The same trapezium decomposition works whichever sloping side is known, including when the calculated height is irrational.
protectedGroups.varies: The side carrying the known leg length, the measurements, and whether the height is integral.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two supplied overhangs, a supplied top base, perpendicular constructions, and the sequence of finding height, complete base, opposite leg and area.

protectedGroups.observation: Pythagoras and the rhombus diagonal formula give the same square area.
protectedGroups.invariant: The square and its 20 cm diagonal.

sequences.title: Area of composite figures with special quadrilaterals

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct: offsets of 2 cm give 98 cm², and offsets of 1 cm give 105 cm². It is dropped under the four-suggestion booklet limit: the other four suggestions more directly expose central area relationships, while this chiefly repeats the inferred-side calculation and reverses it.

candidates.finding: Change the equal offsets while retaining the upper side and perpendicular height.
